An indeterminate is a formal symbol: polynomial equality means equality of all coefficients,
not merely agreement after evaluating on a specified set. Distinct polynomials can induce the
same function over a finite field. Pointwise operations mean (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) and
(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x), not f(g(x)). Over a commutative unital ring, a polynomial is a unit exactly
when its constant coefficient is a unit and all higher coefficients are nilpotent; nonconstant units
are therefore possible when the coefficient ring has nonzero nilpotents.

question.text:
In Z [x], which polynomial is a unit?
4
(A) 1 + x (B) 2 (C) 2 + x (D) 1 + 2x (E) x

solution.text:
2
The identity (1 + 2x) = 1 holds modulo four. A unit must have unit constant coefficient and
nilpotent nonconstant coefficients; 1 + x fails the latter requirement.

question.text:
In the ring C([−1, 1], R) under pointwise operations, let f(x) = max(x, 0) and g(x) =
max(−x, 0). Which statement is correct?
(A) f and g are both units.
(B) f + g is a unit.
(C) f and g are nonzero elements with f g = 0.
(D) f ◦ g equals fg as functions.
(E) fg is the constant function one.

solution.text:
Both functions are continuous and nonzero. At each x, at least one is zero, so their point-
wise product vanishes. Their sum is |x|, which vanishes at zero and is not a unit. Moreover
f ◦ g = g, not the zero function, illustrating why composition is not the multiplication in this
ring.
